question: Fractional CRO vs full-time CRO — which should I hire?
body:
## Direct Answer
Hire a fractional CRO when you need senior revenue leadership for 10 to 25 hours a week to fix a specific problem such as broken forecasting, a stalled go to market motion, or a founder who is still running sales personally. Hire a full time CRO when revenue is above roughly 15 to 20 million dollars, the org is scaling multiple teams, and the job is a permanent seat that owns quota, culture, and board level accountability every day. The decision is really about stage, budget, and whether your core need is a fix or a franchise.

Most founders frame this as a talent question when it is actually a timing and scope question. A fractional Chief Revenue Officer and a full time CRO carry the same title and often the same résumé, but they solve different problems at different price points. Below we break down the cost math, the stage signals, the risk profile, and a decision framework so you can pick the model that matches where your company actually is right now — not where you hope it will be in 18 months.

## What is the real difference between a fractional CRO and a full time CRO?
A full time CRO is a permanent executive who owns the entire revenue engine — sales, marketing alignment, customer success, revenue operations, and forecasting — as a single accountable leader reporting to the CEO. They sit on the leadership team, carry the number, hire and fire their org, and are measured on quarter over quarter growth. This person is all in on one company, present daily, and compensated with a full base salary plus variable plus meaningful equity. The value is total ownership and continuity: they live with the consequences of every decision and build a durable system over years.

A fractional CRO delivers the same strategic seniority on a part time, contracted basis — typically a set number of days or hours per month across an engagement of three to twelve months. They are hired to diagnose and fix rather than to permanently own. Common mandates include installing a repeatable sales process, building the first real forecast, standing up a RevOps function, coaching a promoted first time VP of Sales, or bridging the gap after a departure while you run a search. Because they split time across two to four clients, they bring pattern recognition from many companies but cannot be in every internal conversation. The tradeoff is breadth and speed of expertise versus depth of daily presence. For a deeper primer on the role itself, see our explainer at https://pulserevops.com/knowledge/q10233.

The single most important distinction is the deliverable. A full time CRO delivers an *organization* — teams, culture, and a compounding revenue machine. A fractional CRO delivers a *capability* — a process, a system, a trained leader, or a documented playbook that stays behind when they leave. Confusing the two is the most common hiring mistake founders make, because they hire a fractional expecting permanent ownership, or hire a full time expecting a quick fix and then wonder why the six figure salary did not pay back in one quarter.

## When does a fractional CRO make more sense than a full time hire?
Choose fractional when the problem is bounded and the company is still finding its shape. If you are between roughly 1 million and 10 million dollars in revenue, a full time CRO is usually premature — you do not yet have enough sales headcount, deal volume, or process maturity to keep a senior executive fully occupied, and you cannot yet afford the total package without starving product and hiring. A fractional leader gives you the strategic altitude to build the foundation at a fraction of the burn, so the eventual full time hire inherits a working system instead of chaos.

Fractional also wins when you need a specific transformation on a clock. Classic triggers include a founder led sales team that has plateaued because the founder is the bottleneck, a first time VP of Sales who needs executive coaching to grow into the role, a messy tech stack and no reliable forecast, or a fundraise where investors want to see revenue rigor before writing a check. In each case you need senior judgment for a season, not a permanent chair. A good fractional operator will actively work to make themselves unnecessary — building the process, training the team, and documenting the playbook so the capability survives their exit. Our guide to building a repeatable sales motion at https://pulserevops.com/knowledge/q10891 covers the artifacts a strong fractional should leave behind.

The diagram below shows the typical decision gate most founders walk through.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  A[Need senior revenue leadership] --> B{Revenue above 15M and scaling teams}
  B -->|Yes| C[Hire full time CRO]
  B -->|No| D{Is the need a bounded fix or coaching}
  D -->|Yes| E[Hire fractional CRO]
  D -->|No| F{Can you fund full package without starving product}
  F -->|Yes| C
  F -->|No| E
  E --> G[Build process and train leaders]
  G --> H[Convert to full time when scale demands it]
```

There is also a hybrid path many companies underrate: start fractional, then convert. A fractional engagement is a low risk audition. If the operator fits your culture and the company grows into needing daily ownership, some fractional CROs convert to full time or help you hire and onboard their permanent replacement. This staged approach de risks the single most expensive people decision most early companies make.

## When is a full time CRO worth the commitment and cost?
A full time CRO earns their seat when revenue complexity outgrows part time attention. The clearest signal is scale: multiple sales teams or segments, a growing customer success org, an established marketing function that needs tight alignment, and a board that expects a single throat to choke on the number. Once you are managing dozens of quota carrying reps across regions or product lines, the coordination load alone justifies a daily executive. Part time leadership starts to break down when the cost of a leader *not* being in the room — during a pricing crisis, a key rep resignation, or a board escalation — exceeds the savings of the fractional model.

Timing to the growth curve matters as much as the raw revenue number. Companies preparing for a Series B or later round, planning a material headcount expansion, or entering new markets need someone who will live with the multi year consequences of today's decisions on comp plans, territory design, and culture. A fractional operator optimizes for the engagement window; a full time CRO optimizes for the franchise. Equity is the mechanism that aligns them to the long game — a full time CRO with meaningful ownership is betting years of their career on your outcome, which changes how they hire, how they set quota, and how hard they defend the culture. For how equity and comp design shape executive incentives, see https://pulserevops.com/knowledge/q11002.

The honest counterweight is cost and risk. A full time CRO is one of the most expensive hires a company makes, and a bad one is brutally costly — not just the compensation, but the wrong reps hired, the wrong process installed, the quarters lost, and the severance. Executive search fees, a multi month ramp before they are productive, and the opportunity cost of a mis hire mean the full time route should be a deliberate, well timed decision, not a reflex because a competitor has a CRO or because the title sounds like maturity. If you cannot clearly articulate a full time, permanent mandate that will keep a senior executive occupied and accountable every single day, you are probably not ready yet.

## How do the total costs actually compare?
Cost comparison is where founders most often deceive themselves, because they compare a fractional day rate to a full time base salary and stop there. The real comparison is *total cost of the revenue leadership capability*, and it has three layers. A full time CRO's true cost is base salary plus variable or bonus plus equity plus benefits, payroll taxes, and the fully loaded overhead of a senior seat — the headline salary is often only 60 to 70 percent of the real annual number. A fractional CRO is a contracted fee with no benefits, no equity dilution, no payroll burden, and no severance exposure, and you can scale the engagement up or down as needs change.

But cost per hour is the wrong lens. The right lens is cost per unit of outcome. A fractional CRO at a meaningful monthly retainer can be dramatically cheaper in absolute dollars while still delivering the specific fix you need — if the fix is genuinely bounded. Where fractional gets expensive is scope creep: if you keep expanding the mandate until the fractional operator is effectively doing a full time job at a part time cadence, you get the worst of both worlds — daily problems with part time coverage, and a blended cost that rivals a full time hire without the ownership or equity alignment. The table your finance team should build compares not rates but *total annual spend against the concrete outcome each model is accountable for*.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  A[Revenue leadership need] --> B[Fractional path]
  A --> C[Full time path]
  B --> D[Monthly retainer]
  B --> E[No equity and no benefits]
  B --> F[Flexible scope and easy exit]
  C --> G[Base plus variable]
  C --> H[Equity grant]
  C --> I[Benefits and payroll load]
  D --> J[Compare total annual spend to outcome]
  G --> J
  H --> J
  I --> J
```

One more cost factor is switching and continuity risk. A full time CRO who leaves after a year takes institutional knowledge with them and triggers a costly search and re ramp. A fractional engagement is designed to transfer knowledge into your team and documentation, so continuity lives in your org rather than in one person's head. When you model cost, price in the probability and cost of turnover for each path — it often narrows the gap more than the raw compensation numbers suggest. Our RevOps budgeting walkthrough at https://pulserevops.com/knowledge/q10744 shows how to build this fully loaded comparison.

## What are the biggest risks and failure modes of each model?
The dominant fractional failure mode is *shallow presence on a problem that turned out to be deep*. Because a fractional CRO splits time across clients, they can miss the internal politics, the quiet under performer, or the cultural friction that only surfaces in daily hallway context. If your real problem is not a missing process but a broken team or a founder who will not let go of control, a fractional operator can install a beautiful playbook that dies the moment they leave because no one internally owned the change. Fractional works when there is an empowered internal counterpart — a VP, a head of RevOps, a committed founder — who absorbs the transfer. Without that partner, you are renting expertise that walks out the door with nothing retained.

The dominant full time failure mode is *hiring the seat before the company is ready to feed it*. A full time CRO hired too early is under utilized, gets bored, starts building org structure the company cannot yet support, and burns cash while inventing work. The other classic is the pedigree mis hire: a leader whose experience was scaling a company from 50 to 500 million dollars is often the wrong person to find product market fit or build a first repeatable motion from scratch — different stage, different muscle. Stage-fit matters more than logo prestige. And because full time executive mis hires are so expensive and slow to unwind, the downside is measured in quarters, not weeks.

There is a shared failure mode worth naming: hiring *any* CRO to avoid the CEO's own accountability for revenue. Neither model absolves the founder from owning the number, understanding the funnel, and staying close to customers. A CRO — fractional or full time — is a force multiplier on a CEO who is engaged, and a very expensive scapegoat for one who is not. Before you hire either, make sure the mandate is real, the internal ownership is defined, and leadership is aligned on what success looks like in 90, 180, and 365 days. That clarity, more than the fractional versus full time choice itself, determines whether the hire pays off.

## Related questions
### Can a fractional CRO convert to a full time CRO later?
Yes, and it is a smart de risking path. A fractional engagement acts as a working audition; if the operator fits your culture and the company grows into daily needs, conversion or a smooth handoff to a hire they help recruit is common.

### What revenue level should trigger a full time CRO hire?
There is no hard line, but the common signal band is roughly 15 to 20 million dollars in revenue with multiple scaling teams. Below that, the seat is often under utilized and a fractional or strong VP of Sales usually fits better.

### Is a fractional CRO the same as a sales consultant?
No. A consultant typically advises and produces recommendations; a fractional CRO takes operational ownership of the revenue function during the engagement — running forecasts, coaching leaders, and being accountable for outcomes, not just decks.

### Do I need a CRO or just a VP of Sales?
If your need is executing a known motion and managing reps, a VP of Sales is usually right. A CRO owns the whole revenue engine across sales, marketing alignment, and success, and is warranted when that cross functional coordination is the actual problem.

### How long should a fractional CRO engagement last?
Most run three to twelve months. Shorter than three rarely allows real change to land; longer than twelve often signals scope creep that should be resolved by hiring full time or handing the capability to an internal owner.

## FAQ
**What does a CRO actually own that a VP of Sales does not?**
A CRO owns the entire revenue engine end to end — sales, marketing alignment, customer success, revenue operations, forecasting, and pricing strategy — as a single accountable leader. A VP of Sales typically owns the sales team and its quota within that larger system.

**How many hours per week does a fractional CRO typically work?**
Engagements commonly run in the range of one to three days a week, often expressed as a set number of hours or days per month. The exact cadence is negotiated to the scope of the fix rather than a fixed standard.

**Will a fractional CRO get equity?**
Usually not, or only a small advisory grant. The absence of meaningful equity is a core cost difference — it keeps the fractional model cheaper and more flexible, but it also means less long term alignment than a full time CRO carries.

**Can a small startup afford any kind of CRO?**
Often yes, in fractional form. The fractional model exists specifically so companies that cannot fund a full loaded executive seat can still access senior revenue leadership for a bounded period at a contracted fee.

**What is the number one sign I hired the wrong model?**
For fractional: the playbook dies the moment they leave because no one internally owned it. For full time: the executive is under utilized and inventing org structure the company cannot yet support. Both trace back to a mandate that did not match the stage.

**Does hiring a CRO mean the CEO stops owning revenue?**
No. A CRO multiplies an engaged CEO's effectiveness but never absolves the founder from owning the number, understanding the funnel, and staying close to customers. Treating a CRO as a way to offload accountability is a reliable path to an expensive failure.

**How do I structure a fractional engagement so knowledge is retained?**
Assign an empowered internal counterpart — a VP, head of RevOps, or committed founder — to absorb every process, playbook, and forecast. Require documented deliverables so the capability lives in your org rather than in the operator's head.

**Should I hire a fractional CRO before a fundraise?**
It is a common and effective use case. Investors want to see revenue rigor — a real forecast, a repeatable motion, clean metrics — and a fractional CRO can install that discipline faster and cheaper than a full time search during a capital raise.
